# Implement block: Sundial Time Picker (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Sundial Time Picker" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A calendar's time picker, "Meridian - Pick a time": a limestone horizontal sundial seen from above, with carved hour, half-hour and quarter lines, Roman numerals and a bronze gnomon, under a dashed sky arc with the sun on it. Drag the sun along the arc, or drag the shadow round the dial: the gnomon's shadow swings to that time, shortens towards noon and stretches in the morning and late afternoon, and the light, the stone and the backdrop warm when the sun is low. The time snaps to quarter hours with a tick, and the readout rolls ("15:30"), with the sun's altitude and the end of the 45-minute event under it.

**Motion.** LOOP 9 s, every frame a pure function of t. 0-1.4 rest at 10:00. 1.2-1.4 a fingertip ring lands on the sun. 1.4-4.4 drag to 15:30 (ease-in-out); the readout rolls through every quarter. 4.4 snap: a 6-minute overshoot that dies away by 4.7. 4.4-5.6 hold. 5.6-7.6 back to 10:00 (ease-in-out), the finger lifts at 7.6. 7.6-9 rest. The sun follows an equinox day at latitude 40 deg N (hour angle 15 deg per hour); the dial is a true horizontal sundial, so the shadow of the style lands on the hour line atan(sin 40 deg tan h) that is carved for it. Rendering: one shader for the backdrop, the arc and sun handle, the dial's drop shadow, the limestone (fbm mottling, pits, lichen, a chamfered edge), V-grooved lines lit by the sun's real direction, carved rings, the gnomon (lit on the side facing the sun) and its shadow (the triangle from the gnomon's foot, its tall end and that end's shadow, with a penumbra that widens with distance); the numerals are text recorded once into a picture. Touch: a drag on the dial points the shadow at the finger, a drag above it moves the sun along the arc; the time follows the finger (rubber band past 7:00 and 17:00); a selection haptic ticks at every quarter hour; on release it springs (response 0.45 s, damping ratio 0.7) to the quarter its momentum carries it to. 2 s after the last touch it eases back to 10:00 in 0.9 s and the loop restarts. Hours roll digit by digit, minutes and the end time roll in clipped boxes. Reduced motion: 10:00, still; dragging still works.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [SundialTimePickerDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Pickers/SundialTimePicker/SundialTimePickerDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [SundialTimePicker.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Pickers/SundialTimePicker/SundialTimePicker.metal)
- [SundialTimePicker.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Pickers/SundialTimePicker/SundialTimePicker.swift)
- [SundialTimePickerMotion.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Pickers/SundialTimePicker/SundialTimePickerMotion.swift)
- [SundialTimePickerRoll.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Pickers/SundialTimePicker/SundialTimePickerRoll.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
